body:
I will say in defense of godot btw ... _it is somewhat helped by the fact that I actually put in effort into polishing the lighting_ in godot that I did not do in blender, but like **it mostly looks better and even somewhat more realistic than cycles** out of the box.

I am genuinely blown away.

But the highlights being too bright is such a jarring thing in this scene in particular because it has lamps that reflect in the TV and also the windows.

For the record: I originally incorrectly reported this as #111489. I think the title of that issue is somewhat misleading because and there have been many red herrings in the discussion so again it feels more productive to start over. Also: it has been said that this brightness issue is "the same issue" as #111457 and I disagree. I would love to see both be resolved by the same PR, but I don't think there's much use in creating a big meta issue called "godot specular highlights are weird" I think the stretching of specular highlights that I mentioned is visible in the comparisons I included, but even when the specular highlights are not at all stretched due to the reflection angle, the high specular brightness is still quite noticeable. Godot: Eevee: > **_Please try to not mention the sizes and shapes of the reflections. There has been a whole argument. You can go in the other issue and try to salvage it or create a new better one. I can live with the shapes being weird, it's actually very hard to see if you're not looking for it._**

Note that the specular amount is defined here for Forward+ (note that both `specular_amount` and `specular_amount_highp` are read in the function):

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/c7b176756073ad974be797bc8d039b1628f1264a/servers/rendering/renderer_rd/shaders/scene_forward_lights_inc.glsl#L121

The light's size is the `A` parameter in the `light_compute()` function. We could try to normalize the specular amount by reducing it as the size increases, in a fashion similar to https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/108219. I'm not sure what the formula would look like though, probably an inverse/inverse square function?.

It seems changes to this function aren't being picked up when I recompile and open the editor in Forward+ though. I've even tried to multiply the value by `0.0` and it appears to have no effect.

On top of that, it seems the specular lobe's size doesn't change when using Mobile, as I reported in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/111894. The NaNs that happen when the roughness is exactly `0.0` could hint at the formula needing some kind of clamping too.

> It seems changes to this function aren't being picked up when I recompile and open the editor in Forward+ though. I've even tried to multiply the value by `0.0` and it appears to have no effect.

Okay there seem to be a lot of oddities in this specular highlight.

I have also observed these two behaviors:
 - #111902
 - #111899 (this one is another re-draft of an issue I already reported)

This time I did my best to include more helpful comparisons from the start.

Maybe this could use a meta issue. I am unfortunately not entirely done with the specular oddities yet.

I am currently considering if this could have a common reason and I would love to investigate this.

However it is very difficult to get to the root of this as gdsl does not expost the size property of incoming light as afaik.

Perhaps it will be useful to solve this problem; I recently found this tool for visualizing/analyzing BRDF implementations, although I haven't had the opportunity to test it directly [Disney BRDF Explorer](https://github.com/wdas/brdf).

For most cases, Godot's default implementation is quite good, although I suppose that to obtain a result more similar to Blender's lighting or more "realistic", it is necessary to write a custom shader based directly on the lighting of that program. However, the current lighting models are still incomplete. :p
It's really subtle, but what @betalars says is correct. FullOrenNayar render with LIGHT_COLOR (Stanford Dragon vs SliceImage): BurleyGGX fixed (Stanford Dragon vs SliceImage):
I think this is a better comparison: Godot Standard Material. Using LIGHT_COLOR. Normalized LIGHT_COLOR.

Thank you so much @ElSuicio for confirming this and figuring out some ways to solve this. I have not been able to do much with godot in the past few months, but after finally being able to get back into it and immediately stumbling across this issue again, I am very happy that you took a crack at it.

@betalars, I've found the reason why this isn't a bug. I know it's strange, but from what I understand, Godot internally multiplies the result of LIGHT_COLOR by PI, Making each light unit PI is for compatibility purposes. You might want to check out this [Reddit thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/godot/comments/1rq0xyc/disney_pbs_on_godot/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=mweb3x&utm_name=mweb3xcss&utm_term=1&utm_content=share_button).

P.S. If you want to achieve the same result, you may need to create your own custom shader and simply divide LIGHT_COLOR by PI, I think the best thing would be to create a constant that stores the value of 1.0 divided by PI and multiply that constant by LIGHT_COLOR.

@ElSuicio So I have more thoroughly looked into your observations and I don't think they quite match the issue I am having.

As far as I know, it is also not possible to fix this issue outside of recompiling godot, because light size is something you cannot use in a GDSL shader.
